name: COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and vaccination intent
author: Human Not Found
description: Original study: Loomba, S., de Figueiredo, A., Piatek, S. J., de Graaf, K., & Larson, H. J. (2021). Measuring the impact of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on vaccination intent in the UK and USA. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(3), 337-348. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial with 8,001 respondents in the UK and the US in September 2020, people stated whether they would accept a COVID-19 vaccine, were shown five recent social media posts containing vaccine misinformation or five factual posts, and stated their intent again. Misinformation lowered intent relative to the factual posts. This template runs the US arm with ten US participants: intent before (the original 4-point item), five posts with questions about trust and sharing, and intent after. The posts are new, written for this template, paraphrasing claims that circulated in 2020; the original used real posts with images. The intent-change measure is the share answering 'Yes, definitely' after minus before; compare it between the conditions. Participants are simulated: each is a Model participant, using the free test model until you choose a model, so the first runs only check the design; with the test model every participant takes the sample answer.

overrides.value: It is September 2020. Here are five posts you might see on social media about a coronavirus vaccine. Post 1: 'Coronavirus vaccine trials have enrolled tens of thousands of volunteers to test safety and effectiveness.' Post 2: 'mRNA vaccines teach cells to make a harmless protein; they do not enter the nucleus or change your DNA.' Post 3: 'Vaccines are reviewed by independent regulators before they are approved for use.' Post 4: 'Common side effects of vaccines include a sore arm and tiredness for a day or two.' Post 5: 'Getting vaccinated also helps protect people who cannot be vaccinated, such as some cancer patients.' Answer the questions about them.

spec.description: Ten US participants state vaccination intent before and after seeing misinformation or factual posts.

items.prompt: If a new coronavirus vaccine became available, would you accept it for yourself?
Overall, how trustworthy do these posts seem? 1 = not at all, 5 = very.
How likely would you be to share posts like these? 1 = very unlikely, 5 = very likely.
